title: Apostolic and Disciple Writings — Unified Historical Collection
ordering: Historical events and settings represented by the apostolic- and disciple-associated writings control the order, never composition dates. The Greek/Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter is immediately before Revelation. Revelation is the final record. The Coptic Apocalypse of Peter is a separate work, placed by its own narrative setting.
scope: All identifiable writings connected by historical attribution, claim, tradition, subject, or early community use to apostles and disciples, including gospels, letters, testimony, acts, instruction, apocalypses, and other related writings. Inclusion is not an endorsement of authenticity, apostolic authorship, inspiration, or historical accuracy.
anti_compilation_rule: Do not use the later 27-writing compilation as the archive boundary or as the ordering template. Preserve its history as one later classification only.
date_policy: Composition date estimates are stored separately from physical witness dates. Use null for undetermined dates; never use numeric sentinels. Where estimates overlap or are disputed, show a date band and mark sequence as approximate.
evidence_policy: Every entry must distinguish title tradition, actual author identification, date of composition, earliest surviving witness, manuscript text status, and historical reliability. Anonymous or pseudonymous works must not be presented as verified apostolic authorship. New additions include scholarly research-source URLs. A source supports only the claims described in its entry; it does not automatically verify every textual or attribution statement.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous Gospel of Mark; surviving in the third-century Greek papyrus codex P45

Approximately thirty leaves survive from a much larger original codex, and many are damaged. The Mark passage ranges are fragmentary; they must not be presented as complete chapters or continuous text.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The surviving Mark fragments preserve portions of several episodes in the Lord's ministry, including the storm at sea, healings, the sending of the Twelve, the feeding accounts, disputes and teaching, and events in Jerusalem. This is only a thematic guide to the passages represented; it does not fill gaps or reproduce wording absent from the papyrus.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Editorial content summary based on the published list of surviving passages. It is not a verbatim translation, a reconstruction of missing lines, or a diplomatic transcription of P45.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous Gospel of Mark; preserved in the fourth-century Greek papyrus witness P88
surviving_fragments.passage: Mark 2:1–26 (represented across four pages of a papyrus bifolium)
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The four-page bifolium is divided across Mark 2:1–8, 2:8–15, 2:15–19, and 2:20–26. The represented episodes include the healing of the paralytic and the dispute about forgiveness, the call of Levi and the meal with tax collectors, the question about fasting, and the sayings about new cloth and wineskins.
surviving_fragments.status: P88 (P. Med. Inv. Nr. 69.24) is a separate fourth-century papyrus witness from the third-century P45 codex. It is one papyrus sheet folded as the central bifolium of a quire, forming four pages of approximately 24 × 15 cm, in one column with 22–23 lines per page. The four pages represent Mark 2:1–8, 2:8–15, 2:15–19, and 2:20–26. The manuscript is poorly preserved in places, and two additional correcting hands have been reported. The fourth-century date is the standard catalogue dating, not an exact year.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The surviving section covers several connected episodes: a paralysed man is brought to the Lord and healed; the Lord calls Levi and eats with tax collectors; questions arise about fasting; and the Lord uses images of new cloth and new wine to address the mismatch between old and new forms. This is a content guide to the represented passage, not a translation of the papyrus.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Editorial content summary based on the published description of P88. It is not a verbatim transcription or a reconstruction of damaged wording.

records.description: Its only known manuscript is the damaged Coptic tractate 3 of Codex Tchacos, pages 33–58; the Greek original is inferred, not extant. The text presents conversations between Jesus and his disciples, a special revelation to Judas, and Judas' final handing over of Jesus. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.31.1, separately reports a group using a Gospel of Judas; this is ancient testimony, not a second manuscript or a direct quotation from Codex Tchacos. The title does not establish authorship by Judas.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous Coptic translator and copyist; Codex Tchacos witness
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The single surviving manuscript witness preserves a damaged dialogue gospel. The narrative opens by describing secret teaching Jesus gives Judas over a period of days before Passover. Jesus criticizes the disciples' worship and understanding, gives Judas a revelation concerning heavenly realms and cosmic origins, and the work ends with Judas handing Jesus over to the authorities. The manuscript is damaged and some readings depend on editorial reconstruction.
surviving_fragments.status: Principal and only currently known manuscript witness; damaged Coptic translation. The Greek composition behind it is inferred, not extant in a Greek manuscript.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The text presents Jesus in conversation with the disciples and, more privately, with Judas. Jesus challenges the disciples' understanding and discloses to Judas a vision of heavenly powers, cosmic origins, and the fate of different human generations. The narrative concludes with Judas handing Jesus over. This is a broad content paraphrase of the surviving Coptic work, not a claim that every damaged line is recoverable.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Irenaeus reports that a group he calls Cainites used a writing called the Gospel of Judas and describes their interpretation of Judas. surviving_fragments.status: Ancient bibliographic and polemical testimony; not a manuscript witness or direct quotation from the Gospel.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Irenaeus says that the group he calls Cainites claimed that Judas knew the truth and carried out the mystery of the betrayal, and that they used a Gospel of Judas to support their position. This is Irenaeus' hostile report of the group's teaching, kept distinct from the surviving Coptic narrative.

records.description: The Coptic Apocalypse of Peter is a distinct revelatory dialogue preserved in Nag Hammadi Codex VII, tractate 3, pages 70.13–84.14. Its fourth-century Coptic manuscript is the only known witness. The narrative presents Peter receiving instruction and visions from Jesus in a Jerusalem temple setting, including a distinctive account of Christ's mission and suffering and criticism of rival Christian interpretations. It must not be confused with the separate Greek/Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter. The catalogue summary is not a verbatim translation.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous Coptic translator and copyist; Nag Hammadi Codex VII, tractate 3
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The sole known witness preserves a complete tractate-length apocalypse. The narrative opens with Peter in a temple setting in Jerusalem and presents Jesus as the revealer who guides Peter through visions and instruction. The work develops its distinctive account of Christ, the Saviour's mission, the nature of his suffering, and criticism of groups the author regards as mistaken in their understanding of Christ and the apostolic message. It is a separate work from the Greek/Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter.
surviving_fragments.status: The tractate is preserved across pages 70.13–84.14 of the fourth-century papyrus codex. The manuscript is described as legible and substantially complete, though the Coptic wording contains grammatical difficulties and some physical damage. No second manuscript witness or independent ancient quotation is currently identified.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Peter receives a revelation from Jesus in a Jerusalem temple setting. Jesus explains matters concerning his identity and mission and leads Peter through visions that challenge rival interpretations of the Saviour and the meaning of his suffering. The work presents its own theological claims through a dialogue between Jesus and Peter. This is a summary of the Coptic tractate, not a verbatim translation or a reconstruction of its damaged or difficult wording.

records.description: Letter of Peter to Philip is an anonymous post-resurrection revelatory dialogue framed at its opening as a letter from Peter to Philip. It survives in two Coptic witnesses: Nag Hammadi Codex VIII, tractate 2, and Codex Tchacos, tractate 1. The versions are broadly comparable but contain variants. The Greek original is inferred, not extant. The text depicts the disciples' reunion, prayer, revelation by the Saviour, and renewed mission. The title's letter framing does not authenticate apostolic authorship.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous Coptic translator and copyist; Nag Hammadi Codex VIII witness
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The work opens with a letter framed as Peter's message to Philip, urging the disciples to reunite and proclaim the salvation they received. The narrative then depicts the disciples gathering on the Mount of Olives, praying, and receiving a revelation from the Saviour. The dialogue discusses the nature of the rulers and the creation of the visible world, the Saviour's descent, and the disciples' mission. It closes with their return to Jerusalem and renewed proclamation.
surviving_fragments.status: Principal Coptic witness; comparatively well preserved, with identified lacunae at several lines.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Peter writes to Philip because Philip has been separated from the other disciples. After they reunite, the group prays and receives a revelation from the Saviour. The ensuing dialogue explains the opposition of the rulers, the Saviour's descent, and the disciples' commission to preach. The narrative ends by describing their return to Jerusalem to continue their mission.

records.historical_anchor_basis: Colossians presents Paul as imprisoned (4:3, 10, 18) and names Tychicus as the courier with Onesimus (4:7–9). Ephesians also names Tychicus (Eph 6:21–22), but that shared courier does not by itself prove a single dispatch or identical authorship. No exact order among the prison letters is asserted.

records.historical_anchor_basis: The writing presents Paul as a prisoner in Rome (2 Timothy 1:16–17; 2:9), facing a further hearing after an earlier defense at which no one supported him (4:16–18). It recalls a recent itinerary involving Troas, where a cloak and writings were left with Carpus (4:13), and Miletus, where Trophimus was left ill, while Erastus remained at Corinth (4:20). Timothy is urged to come before winter (4:9, 21). These details form an internal travel-and-imprisonment sequence, but they do not independently establish a second Roman imprisonment after Acts 28. Pauline authorship and the date are disputed; some reconstructions place the setting within Paul's lifetime, while others understand it as a later Pauline-style farewell writing.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Papias' preface explaining how he gathered and evaluated reports from elders and disciples.
surviving_fragments.status: Presented by Eusebius as words from Papias' own preface; surviving through Eusebius, not an independent Papias manuscript.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Papias says he will record what he carefully learned from the elders and remembers accurately. He preferred teachers of truth over people who merely spoke at length. When someone who had followed the elders came, he asked what Andrew, Peter, Philip, Thomas, James, John, Matthew, and the other disciples had said, and what Aristion and the presbyter John were saying. He valued the living, continuing voice more than information obtained from books.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Careful English paraphrase, not a verbatim translation.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Papias transmits a statement attributed specifically to the presbyter John about Mark's account.
surviving_fragments.status: Eusebius introduces this as a saying of the presbyter John reported by Papias. It is not a surviving manuscript of Mark's Gospel and does not establish authorship by itself.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The presbyter said that Mark, as Peter's interpreter, accurately wrote down what he remembered of the Lord's words and deeds, though not in sequence. Mark had not personally followed or heard the Lord; later he accompanied Peter, whose teaching was adapted to the needs of his hearers. Mark's concern was neither to omit what he had heard nor to state anything falsely.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Careful English paraphrase of the transmitted report.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: A brief statement attributed to Papias concerning Matthew's collection of the oracles.
surviving_fragments.status: Survives as Eusebius' quotation of Papias. The phrase about the Hebrew language and subsequent interpretation has a debated meaning and should not be expanded into claims the fragment does not establish.

records.description: Attributed to Papias of Hierapolis. The original work is lost; surviving material consists of fragments quoted by later authors. records.description: 1 Clement is an anonymous early Christian letter addressed to the Corinthian community. Its traditional association with Clement of Rome is a historical attribution, not an authorial signature. The work survives in Greek codices, later Greek copies, and Coptic, Syriac, and Latin versional witnesses. The record distinguishes early and late copies, identifies derivative witnesses, and separates the date of a physical manuscript from the proposed date of the translation or composition. The summaries of manuscript sections are not presented as verbatim transcriptions.

surviving_fragments.source_work: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Supplément grec 64
surviving_fragments.content_scope: This fifteenth-century paper manuscript preserves a continuous section from the discussion of the proper ordering of community service through the letter's extended prayer and exhortations. The witness ends during chapter 60.4. Its text is closely affiliated with Codex Hierosolymitanus.
surviving_fragments.status: Late Greek manuscript section; a secondary witness in the transmission history, not an early independent copy.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The surviving portion addresses orderly appointment and service in the community, the need to avoid rivalry, examples of faithfulness, love and repentance, and a lengthy prayer. This is a section-level content summary, not a new translation.

surviving_fragments.source_work: National Library of Greece, EBE MS 1896
surviving_fragments.content_scope: This late manuscript preserves the opening portion of 1 Clement and breaks off during the account of Abraham and Isaac in chapter 31.3. The copyist marks numerous gaps; the manuscript follows Codex Alexandrinus closely, including lacunae inherited from that exemplar.
surviving_fragments.status: Sixteenth- or seventeenth-century Greek witness; derivative of Codex Alexandrinus rather than an independent ancient witness.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The preserved opening recounts the Corinthian community's former good order and present conflict, urges humility and peace, and gives examples of obedience and faith from earlier generations. The manuscript ends before the letter's later discussion of Abraham is complete. This is a section-level summary, not a translation.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: The manuscript preserves a Latin version of 1 Clement. The surviving codex is dated to the eleventh century; the date of the translation is a separate question and remains a scholarly reconstruction.
surviving_fragments.status: Versional manuscript witness; do not date the physical copy by the proposed age of the translation.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The Latin witness transmits the letter's exhortations to the Corinthian community, its appeal for peace and proper communal order, its scriptural examples, and its closing prayer and instructions. This summary describes the work as transmitted, not the exact wording of this particular copy.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Aristides of Athens; preserved in a fourth-century Greek papyrus codex
surviving_fragments.passage: Greek papyrus portions corresponding to Apology 5.5 and 6.1; the wider codex coverage is reconstructed as 4.3–6.2 with substantial lacunae
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The preserved portions belong to the argument that natural elements are not deities. The section on water treats it as created, mutable, and used by human beings; the section on the sun presents it as moving according to an order beyond itself and serving the world under the Creator's authority.
surviving_fragments.status: P.Oxy. XV 1778 and P.Heid. inv. G 1013 are two fragments from the same codex, not independent witnesses. The fragmentary Greek wording is incomplete; the summary identifies the argument from the extant passage and parallel fuller transmission without claiming to restore missing Greek.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Aristides argues that water is a created part of the world rather than a god, because it changes, can be polluted or redirected, and serves human needs. He likewise argues that the sun is not divine: it follows an ordered course and provides light and warmth under the will of the one who governs it.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Editorial content summary, not a verbatim transcription or a reconstruction of missing Greek. The fuller Syriac transmission is a parallel version and must not be mistaken for the wording of this Greek papyrus.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Aristides of Athens; preserved in a separate fourth-century Greek papyrus codex
surviving_fragments.content_scope: A section from the discussion of Christian belief and conduct. In the wider transmitted text, this closing part describes Christians' ethical conduct, their worship and prayer directed to God, discreet acts of generosity, and expectation of the Messiah and future reward.
surviving_fragments.status: A separate Greek codex witness from the codex represented by P.Oxy. XV 1778 and P.Heid. inv. G 1013. The surviving sheet forms two leaves: one contains part of the Apology and the other a selected passage from Song of Songs 5:12–6:10. The surviving portion is fragmentary.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The passage belongs to Aristides' account of Christian life and hope. It presents Christians as people who seek truth, follow moral commandments, care for others without public display, and look toward the Messiah and the promised future reward. This summary describes the wider transmitted context of the passage; it is not a claim that every detail is legible on the papyrus.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Editorial summary of the passage's context, not a verbatim transcription. The limits of the surviving Greek sheet are kept distinct from the fuller Syriac version.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: A dialogue saying attributed to the Gospel of the Egyptians, in which Salome asks about the power of death.
surviving_fragments.status: Clement quotes the saying while arguing against those who reject marriage and childbirth; his framing is not part of the Gospel quotation.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Salome asks how long death will hold power. The answer connects death's continuation with women giving birth. Clement immediately explains that the saying should not be read as calling life or creation evil, but as describing the sequence in which birth is followed by decay.
surviving_fragments.text_type: English paraphrase of Clement's quotation and immediate explanation; Clement's commentary is distinguished from the Gospel saying.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Sayings attributed to Jesus in a dialogue with Salome, including a statement about the works of the female and a response concerning food.
surviving_fragments.status: Clement quotes and interprets these sayings while disputing an ascetic group's use of them. His interpretation must not be silently merged into the quoted material.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: One saying attributed to the Saviour declares that he came to undo the works of the female. In the same discussion Salome is represented as saying that she did well not to bear children, and the Lord answers with an instruction to eat plants while avoiding what is bitter. Clement interprets the imagery in relation to birth and decay; that interpretation is his own explanatory argument.
surviving_fragments.text_type: English paraphrase of the reported sayings with Clement's commentary identified separately.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: A dialogue saying in which Salome asks when the matters under discussion will become known.
surviving_fragments.status: A saying attributed to the Gospel of the Egyptians; Clement compares it with other teachings and uses it in his argument.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Salome asks when the things about which she has questioned will become known. The answer speaks of trampling the garment of shame and of the two becoming one, with male and female no longer divided into those categories.
surviving_fragments.text_type: English paraphrase of the surviving saying.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Hippolytus reports that the Naassenes used the Gospel of the Egyptians and summarizes their teaching about the soul.
surviving_fragments.status: This is a report about a group's use of the Gospel, not a securely identifiable verbatim quotation from the Gospel itself.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Hippolytus says that the Naassenes appealed to the Gospel of the Egyptians while describing the soul as difficult to find and understand, changing in form and condition rather than remaining in one fixed state.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Paraphrase of Hippolytus' report; not presented as a direct Gospel quotation.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Epiphanius reports sayings he associates with the Gospel of the Egyptians in his discussion of Sabellians.
surviving_fragments.status: A later polemical report; it records Epiphanius' characterization and should not be treated as an independently preserved Gospel passage.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Epiphanius claims that the work contains sayings presented as secret teaching of the Saviour and used by the group he is criticizing to support the view that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same. This is Epiphanius' report of their use of the text, not a neutral description of the Gospel's complete teaching.
surviving_fragments.text_type: Paraphrase of a heresiological report, not a verbatim Gospel fragment.

records.description: Gospel of Philip is a Coptic collection of sayings and theological reflections preserved in Nag Hammadi Codex II, tractate 3 (pages 51.29–86.19). It is not a continuous narrative gospel, and its title does not establish authorship by Philip. The Coptic codex is the sole complete textual witness; the original Greek is inferred, not extant. Epiphanius separately quotes a Gospel bearing Philip's name in Panarion 26.13.2–3. That soul-ascent passage does not occur in NHC II,3 and is not inserted into this work.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous compiler; Nag Hammadi Codex II, tractate 3
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The opening portion is a collection of short sayings, comparisons, and reflections. Topics include spiritual transformation, the relationship between the living and the dead, the status of believers, the role of the Saviour, and the interpretation of names and images. It is not a continuous narrative of Philip's life.
surviving_fragments.status: Surviving portion of the sole complete Coptic witness; individual damaged lines and editorial restorations must be checked against the codex edition.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The opening sayings contrast outward status with inward transformation, and repeatedly use images of birth, inheritance, light, and recognition to describe spiritual life. Several sayings are attributed to the Lord or Saviour, while other passages are explanatory reflections by the compiler. This is a section-level summary, not a line-by-line translation.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous compiler; Nag Hammadi Codex II, tractate 3
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The middle portion develops reflections on images, names, truth, and the rites of baptism and anointing (chrism). It includes short sayings and interpretive passages concerning the Saviour, the cross, spiritual rebirth, and the relationship between visible signs and their spiritual realities.
surviving_fragments.status: Surviving portion of the Coptic codex; paragraph divisions and saying numbers vary among modern editions.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The compiler connects ritual actions with transformation and knowledge: baptism and anointing are discussed as meaningful spiritual realities rather than merely external acts. The text also uses images and names to explain how visible things can point beyond themselves. The paraphrase summarizes themes and does not supply missing wording.

surviving_fragments.transmitting_author: Anonymous compiler; Nag Hammadi Codex II, tractate 3
surviving_fragments.content_scope: The closing portion continues reflections on redemption, the bridal chamber, the separation and reunion of human realities, and the relationship between Mary Magdalene and the Saviour. It ends with the title written at the conclusion of the codex text. Some lines in the codex are damaged; reconstructions in translations are editorial.
surviving_fragments.status: Surviving closing portion of the sole complete Coptic witness; damaged places must remain distinguished from preserved text.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: The closing sayings discuss redemption and the bridal chamber through symbolic language of union, restoration, and spiritual completion. Mary Magdalene is described in a special relationship to the Saviour, but the manuscript's damaged wording does not justify filling gaps with popular speculative claims. The text concludes with its title, 'The Gospel according to Philip,' at the end of the work.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Epiphanius quotes a passage he attributes to a Gospel in the name of Philip, describing the soul's ascent past hostile powers after death. This quoted passage is not found in the surviving Gospel of Philip in Nag Hammadi Codex II. Most reference works treat Epiphanius' cited writing as a distinct work with the same or a similar title; its relationship to the Nag Hammadi tractate remains debated.
surviving_fragments.status: Ancient quotation from a separately transmitted work attributed to Philip; not part of NHC II,3 and not a missing passage that can be inserted into it.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: In Epiphanius' report, the ascending soul answers hostile heavenly powers by declaring that it has come to know itself, has gathered itself together, and has not produced offspring for the ruler of this world. Epiphanius presents this as a quotation from a Gospel bearing Philip's name. It is kept separate from the Nag Hammadi Gospel of Philip because it does not occur in that Coptic text.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Clement attributes to the Traditions of Matthias the exhortation to marvel at what is present, describing it as the first step toward knowledge beyond. In the same paragraph Clement separately quotes a saying from the Gospel according to the Hebrews about the one who marvels, reigns, and then rests; that second saying must not be assigned to Matthias.
surviving_fragments.status: Direct saying attributed to the Traditions of Matthias; the nearby Gospel of the Hebrews quotation is a separate source.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Clement says that Matthias, in the Traditions, urges the hearer to marvel at what is present and presents this wonder as the first step toward knowledge of what lies beyond. Clement then introduces a separate saying from the Gospel according to the Hebrews about the one who marvels, reigns, and rests.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Clement reports that Matthias taught disciplined resistance to bodily impulses, refusing to yield to uncontrolled pleasure, so that the soul may grow through faith and knowledge.
surviving_fragments.status: Indirectly introduced saying attributed to Matthias; the wording is preserved by Clement.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Clement says that Matthias taught people to struggle against the flesh and not surrender to uncontrolled pleasure, but to strengthen or increase the soul through faith and knowledge. The phrase about 'abusing' the flesh is contextually explained by Clement as self-control, not as permission for harm.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Clement explicitly says that Matthias the apostle taught this saying about the responsibility of an elect person for the example set before a neighbor.
surviving_fragments.status: Direct saying introduced as a teaching from the Traditions of Matthias.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Clement attributes to Matthias the teaching that when a neighbor of an elect person sins, the elect person is also implicated: if the elect person lived according to the teaching, the neighbor would be ashamed by that example and refrain from sinning.

surviving_fragments.content_scope: Clement reports that certain groups, including Basilideans, claimed an association with Matthias' teaching or tradition; he does not quote a Matthias saying here.
surviving_fragments.status: Heresiological/bibliographic report only; not a surviving fragment of the Traditions of Matthias.
surviving_fragments.english_paraphrase: Clement notes that some groups claimed to follow the teaching or tradition of Matthias, while arguing that apostolic teaching and tradition were one. This passage documents a later claim of affiliation; it does not preserve a saying from Matthias.

records.description: Gospel of Matthias / Traditions of Matthias is a reported sayings collection in the Unified Apostolic and Disciple collection. No complete manuscript survives, and whether the title Gospel of Matthias refers to the same work as the Traditions of Matthias remains uncertain. Clement of Alexandria preserves three sayings attributed to Matthias in Stromateis 2.9.45, 3.4.26, and 7.13.82. Stromateis 7.17.108 is retained only as a later report about groups claiming Matthias' authority, not as a quotation from the work. In Stromateis 2.9.45, Clement also quotes the Gospel according to the Hebrews; the two attributions are kept separate.

records.historical_anchor: John's Patmos setting and messages to seven assemblies in Roman Asia
records.historical_anchor_basis: Revelation 1:4 identifies seven assemblies in the province of Asia; 1:9 places John on Patmos because of the word of God and the witness of Jesus; 1:11 names the seven destinations. Chapters 2–3 address those assemblies, while 22:16 again frames the work as testimony for the assemblies. The text does not identify John as the son of Zebedee, so that identification must remain separate from the stated name. The date is disputed: a late-first-century setting, often associated with Domitian, is widely argued, while some scholarship proposes a date around 68–69 CE under Nero. The language of suffering does not by itself prove an empire-wide official persecution; local pressures and conflicts are also considered. Patmos is the stated location of John's vision, but whether every stage of composition occurred there is not certain.
records.historical_order_note: Final record in the collection by explicit archive arrangement. Its Patmos setting and disputed date remain separate; final placement is not a claim about the chronological fulfilment of every vision.

historical_chronology_policy: Use the events and historical setting represented in each writing as the organizing basis. For narratives, follow narrated events. For letters and instruction writings, use the historical situation, people, journeys, imprisonment, or community events they address. If an exact setting cannot be established, use a broad labelled period and mark placement provisional. Never use composition date as a substitute for event chronology. Revelation is the final catalogue record by explicit archive arrangement; the Greek/Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter is immediately before it. The Coptic Apocalypse of Peter is a separate work placed by its own Jerusalem-before-crucifixion narrative setting.

chronology_policy.primary_rule: Use events narrated or historical situations addressed, not composition or manuscript dates.
chronology_policy.overlapping_narratives: Group accounts covering the same events rather than claiming an unsupported order among them.
chronology_policy.letters: Use internal references, journeys, communities, conflicts and imprisonment settings; mark disputed reconstructions.
chronology_policy.later_accounts: Identify later retellings as later narrative claims, not verified eyewitness chronology.
chronology_policy.uncertainty: An unresolved historical anchor must remain provisional; do not invent exact dates.
chronology_policy.subsequence: The records array is physically ordered by historical_sequence, then historical_subsequence. Equal values mean no exact relative order is asserted; title order is only a neutral display tie-breaker and never uses composition date.
chronology_policy.non_narrative: Sayings collections, sermons and writings without a single event sequence are explicitly identified as not internally chronologically placeable.
chronology_policy.later_claims: Later pseudonymous narratives are placed by the scene they claim to narrate only where a scene is identifiable; this does not authenticate the event.
chronology_policy.unplaced_group: Writings without a sufficiently secure event sequence are shown in a separate final group. This group is not ordered by composition date.

scope_policy.inclusion: This unified catalogue is limited to writings attributed to, associated with, or reporting correspondence of apostles and early disciples, including later works written under their names. Inclusion does not prove authorship. Include fragmentary, lost, hypothetical, pseudonymous, and later writings where an apostolic/disciple connection is claimed or studied, while labelling the strength of evidence. Inclusion does not prove authenticity.
